newsitem.title: UK: LME markets edge off lows, but still end weak.
newsitem.headline: LME markets edge off lows, but still end weak.

text.p: Base metal prices edged above midsession lows during Monday afternoon ring and kerb trading on the LME, but still closed softer than Friday and were seen falling further, traders said.

The modest pick-up from the low points was nothing more substantial than routine jobber covering with little solid buying seen from the trade who were content to hold off given that sentiment is conclusively bearish, they said.
"At the moment the rallies will not go too far as people are looking to sell into them," one trader said.
Copper was again the bell-wether for the complex, although other metals needed little excuse to move lower. Tuesday's inventory data is likely to hold out little overall respite.
Copper confirmed Friday's loss of the $1,900 level with the market trending back to a low point of $1,864 before final business at $1,883, a $17 a tonne decline from Friday's kerb.
Cash/threes narrowed marginally this afternoon to $10/11 contango from $15.
Traders said copper's short-term downside objective is $1,850 if $1,900 cannot be regained. Stocks are seen falling tomorrow but this may not dispel current negative sentiment.
Aluminium's recent run of new lows was maintained today with the market tumbling under the $1,400 level to hit $1,390 at one stage -- another 2-1/4 year low.
Late covering reduced losses, although final business at $1,392 was still $20 down from Friday.
Traders said the market will remain weak, given that consumers are adopting a hand-to-mouth, scale-down buying policy. Also, stocks are on the increase, with LME inventories seen higher on Tuesday.

Tin clawed its way hesistantly off six-month lows of $6,000, although this psychological level is expected to be re-challenged in the short term. Prices finished at $6,030, an $80 loss from pre-weekend levels.

Fundamentally the market is under pressure from the perception that world stocks will be higher at year-end and the likelihood that the current ATPC meeting in Singapore will do little for sentiment, traders added.

Nickel rallied away from midsession lows of $7,200, but remained easier and set for further declines with stocks seen rising again on Tuesday. Last trade was at $7,320, down $60 from the previous kerb close.
Lead's mini-rally arrested an earlier slump to 10-week lows, but this market also seems destined for further price falls. Three months closed at $775, a $7 loss.

Zinc again attracted consumer interest on price dips as well as some support from expectations of another inventory fall tomorrow. However the market will continue to be influenced by copper in the short-term.
Final business was at $1,019, down $11 from Friday.
Alloy traded quietly, finishing $5 lower at $1,225 a tonne.
